analysis.one_liner: Creates a dedicated trust fund, financed by higher corporate taxes, to pay for water and sewer repairs nationwide.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 87 House Democrats and no Republicans, was sent to four House committees and never received a hearing, a vote, or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a dedicated federal trust fund for water and sewer infrastructure, funded by raising the corporate income tax rate from 21% to 24.5%, capped at $34.85 billion per year. The money would flow to state revolving funds for clean water and drinking water, grants to fix or replace septic systems, household wells, lead-contaminated school drinking water fixtures, lead service lines, and water systems contaminated by PFAS chemicals. It would also require states to protect households facing water shutoffs, direct aid to publicly owned water systems, and report on discriminatory practices by water providers.
analysis.who_benefits: Households facing unaffordable water bills, shutoffs, or lead and PFAS contamination in their water; rural families with failing septic systems and private wells; tribal communities; schools with lead-tainted fountains; municipal water systems; and construction workers who would build the projects under prevailing-wage and project-labor rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households with unsafe or unaffordable water

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a trust fund of up to $34.85 billion per year, appropriated automatically from the new corporate tax revenue, for clean water and drinking water programs [S2][S3].
Requires grants to homeowners to repair, replace, or upgrade septic tanks and drainage fields, and expands the rural household water well grant program to $348.5 million per year [S3].

Increases the school drinking water grant program from $5 million to $1.05 billion to make school fountains, coolers, and bottle-filling stations lead-free, and gives homeowners grants to replace lead service lines [S3].

Directs drinking water revolving fund guidance to ensure affordable, equitable water service and protections for households facing disconnection for unpaid water bills, and funds treatment upgrades and household filters for PFAS-contaminated water [S3].

Requires an EPA study, with the Justice Department, on water affordability, disconnections, and discrimination and civil rights violations by water providers, plus a tripling of the tribal drinking water set-aside [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, through a higher corporate income tax rate (21% to 24.5%) that could raise up to $34.85 billion per year. Investor-owned water utilities would also lose: the bill restricts federal loan funds to publicly owned water systems and lets municipalities buy private water systems from a willing or unwilling seller. Nonunion contractors could be disadvantaged by requirements favoring project labor agreements.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporate taxpayers and private water utilities

drawbacks.text: The bill is financed by raising the corporate income tax rate to 24.5%, a broad tax increase on corporate income that economists warn can be partly passed to workers and consumers through lower wages or higher prices [S3].

It authorizes state revolving fund money to purchase privately owned water and sewer systems from a willing or unwilling seller, effectively enabling condemnation of investor-owned utilities, which opponents would call an unfair taking of private property [S3].

It requires state revolving fund projects to be carried out, to the maximum extent practicable, through project labor agreements, which nonunion contractors argue narrows who can bid on publicly funded work [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets real, well-documented harms: lead in school drinking water and household pipes, PFAS contamination, failing septic systems, and water bills households cannot pay. Its dedicated funding stream avoids the annual Appropriations fight, which is why water infrastructure has historically been underfunded. The honest tradeoffs are the broad corporate tax increase to pay for it, the forced-sale authority over private water companies, and project labor agreement preferences that not all contractors welcome. On balance, the benefits are large and broad, and the costs are concentrated and clearly identified.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees and their subcommittees and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 28, 2019 by Rep. Brenda Lawrence of Michigan [S1][S5].
It was referred to four committees: Transportation and Infrastructure, Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Agriculture [S5].
Within days it was further referred to subcommittees on Water Resources and Environment, Environment and Climate Change, and Conservation and Forestry [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill died in committee when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1][S5].
It drew 87 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, and no Republican cosponsor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations kept the 21% corporate tax rate rather than the proposed 24.5%, and investor-owned water utilities faced no risk of forced sale or loss of federal loan eligibility. Households with lead pipes, contaminated wells, and unaffordable water bills received nothing from this bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 87 cosponsors were House Democrats, roughly 38% of the caucus; no Republican cosponsored, and the Democratic chairs of the four committees of referral never scheduled action.

industries.note: The bill would restrict federal revolving fund loans to publicly owned systems and allow municipalities to buy private water and sewer systems from a willing or unwilling seller, threatening the investor-owned water utility business model. Their interest in preserving private ownership ran against the bill's push for public ownership and affordability protections.

industries.industry: Corporate taxpayers (large corporations and their shareholders)
industries.note: The bill raises the corporate income tax rate from 21% to 24.5% to fund up to $34.85 billion per year in water infrastructure. The tax burden would fall on corporations and shareholders rather than on water customers.

industries.industry: Water and sewer construction contractors and materials suppliers
industries.note: The bill would channel tens of billions of dollars a year into water and sewer construction, with Buy American requirements for drinking water materials and prevailing wage and project labor agreement provisions that favor unionized contractors. Their gain comes alongside the public's gain from repaired infrastructure.
